articles.description:
Creativity doesn’t drive my blogging; software does. So daily.baty.net is back in rotation and is once again built using Tinderbox.
Tinderbox is special. I've been preaching this for more than 20 years. However, my use of Tinderbox has slowed down in recent years due to the distraction that is Linux. I felt I needed to move away from macOS-only software. I shouldn't have.
I've been "going ham" with Tinderbox recently, and it feels good. I used to live in its Map views, but that was back when I was working. Now, I use it mostly as a fancy outliner (it's a really good outliner) and as a blogging tool.
Tinderbox manages daily.baty.net. For a minute I was using Eleventy, but no longer. Tinderbox's export features are complex, and sometimes I get lost, but they're also very flexible and powerful.
Long story short, when I'm experiencing the rush that comes with rediscovering Tinderbox, I want to use it for everything, so I brought it back and I'm posting daily notes there instead of journal entries here.
In case you were wondering.
✍️ Reply by email
articles.title: While we're un-retiring things: daily.baty.net and Tinderbox

I miss when a bunch of us weirdos overshared on our TiddlyWikis nearly every day. Most are gone or unmaintained now. Can we bring them back? I'll start: rudimentarylathe.org
Nearly 5,000 notes going back to 2018, and man oh man, at least 4,800 of them are an embarrassment. I should keep this stuff to myself, but that horse left the barn long ago.
We used to write "TiddlyMails" to each other (I don't think we actually called them that). I'd write a note that simply mentioned someone with their own wiki. They'd read it, and write a note on their wiki with a link back and a title something like: "Re: That thing you wrote". It was completely manual and done without pings or notifications of any kind. So fun!
If you have a similar wiki, let me know. I'd love to visit!
TiddlyWiki is more than 20 years old and still a miracle to me.

articles.description:
After last night’s post, I realised I was probably just getting too invested in somehow using imdb for the “who’s that actor, anyway?” command for my Emacs-based video player.
Not only is it an extremely fragile setup that’s gonna stop working, but it’s also very slow — it takes half a minute to return the actor profile images.
So I just implemented a tmdb API shim and then I ask it for the actor profile photo instead.  tmdb doesn’t have as large a data base, but…  The API is free (for non-commercial use) and is extremely easy to use.
Things are now faster:

The main wait is from the response from the LLM — I’m using gemini-3.8-flash.  I’ve tried gemini-3.1-flash-lite, and it’s much faster…  but gives the wrong result most of the time.  No, that’s not Roy Scheider, Gemini!
So now the setup is less Rube Goldberguesque.  Sort of:
I hit a key on my li’l wireless keyboard.

It’s picked up by a Python script that listens for evdev events.

It uses emacsclient to notify the Emacs running on the TV machine.

Emacs there tells mpv to do a screenshot.

Emacs waits until the screenshot arrives on disc.

Emacs sends it to Gemini and says “who dis? JSON please”.

Gemini responds and Emacs then creates an SVG overlay with the actor name.

rsvg-convert converts to PNG and then imagemagick convert to BGRA.

Emacs asks mpv to display it.

Emacs asks tmdb for the actor profile URL and fetches the image.

If it gets a response, it then recreates the svg with the image embedded.

(repeat 8-9).

Couldn’t be simpler.
articles.title: Lars Ingebrigtsen: OK, OK, I’ll just use tmdb

articles.description:
interesting post about BYOK. BYOK is a “writer deck”, a device exclusively for writing that has no distracting apps or even a connection to the Internet. The idea is that writers can’t get distracted when they reach a temporary block by escaping to social media or something similar; they have to push through the block and get on with their writing.


According to Martin, BYOK is better than most devices in its class but there are still problems. He doesn’t like the available fonts and the screen—as you can see from the picture in his post—is pretty small, about 6 lines depending on the font. That seems to me to amount to a rather uncomfortable working environment. Fortunately, I don’t usually find myself distracted when I’m writing.


Then there’s the matter of research. Very often you need to look something up when you’re writing and you can’t do that with something like BYOK so you need to switch devices,  pulling you even further out of the flow. And as Martin observes, it’s not easy to integrate your notes either.


The deal buster for me, though, is the builtin editor. It’s not Emacs based and doesn’t even support Emacs keybindings for navigation. As I’ve repeatedly said—as recently as yesterday—I simply can’t comfortably write outside of Emacs anymore. Martin is a relative newcomer to Emacs but he’s already feeling the discomfort. Once the Emacs way sets in, he’ll be just like me and won’t consider doing serious writing outside of Emacs.


Even if I were subject to being distracted by the greater Internet, I would simply turn off my WiFi to produce what is effectively an Emacs based writer deck. One thing for sure, I’m not giving up Emacs and suffering a second rate writing environment.
articles.title: Irreal: BYOK

articles.description:
And now it’s all this, Dr Drang has a post on using TextEdit versus using Pages. He’s a Mac user, obviously, but that doesn’t matter so much. The real argument is over whether one should use a word processor or some sort of text based editor.


There can be no doubt on where I stand on the issue. The only time I can remember using a “word processor” of any type in the last 3 decades was when I had to collaborate on another author’s file as a technical editor1. As I’ve said before, whenever I write in anything other than Emacs, I feel like I’m in Bizarro World where nothing works as it should. That includes even things like iMessage which is why I tend to use emacs-everywhere for it and most other things.


Dr Drang is nominally the same. He says he almost never uses a Word Processor but sometimes for a one-off he thinks it makes sense to use a word processor rather than one of his LaTeX or Markdown templates. That seems backwards to me. Sure, maybe you don’t want to use a template for a technical report to write a quick note to your baby sitter but Pages or any other word processor is not the simple alternative. I’d simply use Org and export it to whatever format seems appropriate. Even if Dr Drang is not an Emacs user, he is a Markdown user so surely the easy thing for him to do is to dash off his quick note in Markdown.


Really, unless you have collaboration issues, there’s no reason to subject yourself to the horrors of a word processor.


Footnotes: 
1 



That post was so long ago that I was still using Groff instead of Org to typeset documents. I’ve done technical editing since then that also required a Word clone and the experience was no better.
articles.title: Irreal: Why Use A Word Processor When You Have Org?

articles.description:
Journelly. I use it as my memo book to record my daily activities and random things that I want to remember. For example, if I see some article or ad in my browser, I can ask Safari to share it with Journelly and a Journelly entry is automatically made complete with a link to whatever it was I wanted to capture. Each entry contains a date/time stamp as well as the location of where the entry was made.


Best of all, Journelly keeps its data as an Org file so I can query or edit it in Emacs. Of course, Journelly has a search function but sometimes I want to do a more complicated search or even to just count the number of entries in the database (4361 as of right now). Having the database as an Org file means that my data is available on all my devices, even if that device is a Mac.


I’ve been using Journelly since March 2025, ever since it was in beta, and have never looked back. Lately, however, it’s been getting a bit laggy, something I put down to my large database. I was on the verge of truncating my active data to the most recent entries in order to improve performance when Álvaro Ramírez pushed a new beta—v1.5(4)—that completely solved the problem. Now Journelly performs just like it did when I started.


If you are an Emacs user and are using an iPhone/iPad, I can’t think of any reason why you wouldn’t want to use Journelly. It allows you to integrate your day-to-day note taking with the power of Org mode. Even if you aren’t an Emacs user, you’ll probably find Journelly useful. It can also save its data as a markdown file so you can still get all the benefits of an easily accessible and editable database even if you prefer another editor.
articles.title: Irreal: A New Journelly Beta

another step in the journey so many of are on: moving everything inside Emacs. Regular Irreal readers will recall that Ridenour is a Philosophy professor so he doesn’t have much need for high powered math tools but he does have to deal with grade calculations and various budget items. He had been using Soulver for this but, of course, this meant leaving Emacs, something all we Emacers hate.


Then he stumbled on literate-calc-mode. It did everything that Soulver did and Ridenour didn’t have to leave Emacs to use it. It’s been a win for him and he’s happy with it.


When I read Ridenour’s post, something seemed familiar. It turns out that I’d written about literate-calc-mode six years ago. It had just been released and no one had any experience with it yet. I meant to follow up but, of course, life intervened and I never did. I’m glad to see that it’s still around and has lived up to its potential.


I’m tempted to install it but I’m reasonably proficient with Calc itself so I probably wouldn’t use it enough to make it worthwhile. Still, if Reverse Polish Notation is not your thing and you’d rather deal with normal infix notation, literate-calc-mode may be a good fit. It’s easy to try out so give it a spin if you’re interested.

Soulver on the Mac.



I recently stumbled on Literate Calc Mode by Robin1 that does everything I was using Soulver for, and I now have one more reason to not leave Emacs. It’s in Melpa, so installing it is simple. Once required, it provides both literate-calc-mode and literate-calc-minor-mode. I find the minor mode particularly useful for Org mode scratch buffers. For example, I used it recently to sketch out some details for a conference funding request. In an Org buffer, I entered:



Expenses for February 2027 Baylor Trip

Hotel = 500
Parking = 10
Registration = 295
Mileage = 300
Meals = 200

Total = Hotel + Parking + Registration + Mileage + Meals

M-x literate-calc-minor-mode instantly changed it to this:



Expenses for February 2027 Baylor Trip

Hotel = 500 => Hotel: 500
Parking = 10 => Parking: 10
Registration = 295 => Registration: 295
Mileage = 300 => Mileage: 300
Meals = 200 => Meals: 200

Total = Hotel + Parking + Registration + Mileage + Meals => Total: 1,305

=> is not editable and displayed in a lighter shade. Changing one of the variable values results in an instant update of the total. It uses Calc, so it is able to do almost anything that Calc can do. So far, I’ve used it to plan travel expenses and to build material lists for woodworking projects. It works flawlessly and I’ve found it surprisingly useful to have a scratchpad that can automatically do the math.




Tagged:  Emacs




Footnotes
1 

I couldn’t find a last name on the site.

articles.description:
The ability to mark items in GNU Emacs Dired allows for bulk operations on both files and directories. With marking, onerous tasks can be turned into a trivial ones.
While default Dired has many bulk operation commands, not everything is covered. That is the motivation for mdired, an Elisp package which extends Dired with some SIMD-style commands.
Using these commands fall into two steps:
Mark the items of interest in Dired.
Run the mdired command.
mdired supports the following four commands:
mdired-copy: copy a single file to multiple directories.
mdired-do-command: run an Elisp command or named keyboard macro on multiple files.
mdired-compile: run compile on multiple directories.
mdired-byte-recompile: byte-compile selected files or directories.
Refer to the mdired User Guide for more details on usage.
Closing Thoughts
Bulk operation commands are chainsaws. Use them with caution. That said, they are great for improvised workflows:
“Here’s this file that I want copied to a bunch of directories.”
“I want to do the same edit operation on this set of files. I’ve got a named keyboard macro ready to go on them.”
“I want to run the same make command on a bunch of directories.”
As mdired is new, I’m open to feedback on it. Let me know what you think.
mdired v1.0 is now available on MELPA.
articles.title: Charles Choi: Announcing mdired, or adding a chainsaw to Dired

articles.description:
marking the active window (update here ) so that it’s easy to pick it out from the other, inactive windows. I did that by making the mode line of the active window a distinct color instead of the slightly different shade of gray from the other windows. That’s worked out really well for me and I’ve never looked back.


Now Ray Zeitler over at Ray on Emacs takes another look at the problem and found a really nice solution. It’s a bit more in your face than mine so if you’re looking for something that makes the active window really stand out, you should take a look at his post. The TL;DR is that instead of changing the active window, he changes the background color of all the other windows.


Zeitler found his solution on a 10 year old Stack Exchange post so it’s pretty certain to work no matter what version of Emacs you’re using. The code is very simple and you can simply copy it to your init.el if you’re interested.


As I said, this solution seems a little aggressive to me so I doubt I’ll be implementing it but others may disagree. One thing for sure, it’s going to make your active window stand out. It’s a small enough change that you can try it out—say by copying it to your scratch buffer and executing it—to see if it’s something you’d like.
articles.title: Irreal: Highlighting The Active Window

You—yes, you—could be in elected office today. The median Defector reader is a smart and good-looking progressive with impeccable taste. What other qualifications do you really need? Had you thrown your hat in ahead of the blue wave, today you could be your state's lieutenant governor. Hell, for that matter, maybe you are your state's lieutenant governor. Have you checked your mail?
Consider the case of Sebastian Matta. Matta is a 19-year-old sophomore at Arizona State University. He has a 3.25 grade-point average, per the New York Times, and he lives at home with his parents. Starting in February, Matta will be the Superior Court Clerk of Maricopa County, which has a geographic area larger than New Jersey and a population larger than Oregon. Matta will lead a department that, according to Phoenix-area CBS affiliate KTVK, processes more than 16,000 documents per day and has an annual budget of $65 million. Matta will be the boss to some 670 veteran professional staff. 
"I hope that they realize that I’m just not any 19-year-old," said Matta, hoping to give confidence to the hundreds of people who will soon be working under him in an incredibly complex bureaucracy.
articles.title: You Could Be County Clerk, Or Sheriff!

Caleb Williams is carrying an unimaginable burden, and it's not just the matter of being the last living quarterback in the NFL, or easing into his place as the best Chicago Bears quarterback in three quarters of a century while running the most prolific Bears offense in 50 years. It's been only eight weeks since his season began, and already he is the preeminent face of Chicago sports. This looks like high praise, but while that praise would be deserved where Williams is concerned, consider the context.
Williams is not working against a deep field—not in the NFC North, which is the toughest division in the league, but in the town in which he works. There, his opposition is Northwestern's football team, which is 6-2 but unranked and unlikely to break through the upper crust of the Big Ten. The Cubs were routed from the postseason in the shortest possible amount of time, and the White Sox are still striking out despite their season having ended four weeks ago. The Sky are notable only for having turned Angel Reese into a useful player by trading her to another team. And the Bulls and Blackhawks are demonstrably god-awful, well within the margin for error for having a spectacular margin for errors. You know, like the post-election Republican mood.
How god-awful, you ask, since you've been averting your eyes? The Bulls are 1-7, and are losing their games by an average of 18 points per game, which ranks as the largest margin of stinkage in NBA history, albeit in this admittedly minuscule sample; they are allowing the second-highest number of points per game ever. They will doubtless revert to a gentler if still depressing mean, as all non-expansion teams tend to do, but with a starting lineup of Caleb Wilson, Norman Powell, Josh Giddey, Matas Buzelis, and Jalen Smith, it would be foolish to rule out the 11-71 outcome for their season.
articles.title: Caleb Williams Is Carrying All Of Chicago Sports On His Back

articles.author: Albert Burneko
articles.description:
The Tesla car company "will be winding down production of the Cybertruck" in 2027, according to a tweet from Elon Musk. Like everything else Musk says, ever, this must be treated as having essentially no truth value whatsoever and at best a coincidental relationship to anything that later happens with or to Cybertruck production. It's noteworthy as an index of what Musk wants people to believe—it's noteworthy, then, that Musk wants people to believe that the era of Cybertruck production is coming to an end.
And by "noteworthy," I mean: fucking hilarious!
Few vehicles live on in history as metonyms for failure and embarrassment. Edsel, DeLorean, whatever poor beleaguered machine ferries the Sacramento Kings to a given road game instead of doing them the favor of exploding along the way. Add to these the Cybertruck, one of the most hyped vehicles of all time; Tesla's production capacity for the Cybertruck reportedly was something like 250,000 units per year, and, should the end of its production in fact come in 2027, it will wrap up its four-year run certainly having sold, in total, worldwide, under half of that number. Given the ballooning demand for electric vehicles, the relative lack of competition among all-electric trucks, Tesla's huge head-start in EV production, the unparalleled hype around the Cybertruck's release, and its flowering into a rolling emblem of Musk's personal toxicity, the Cybertruck deserves to endure in history as among the most embarrassing mass-produced products ever available for purchase by human beings. I'd rather carry a battery-powered Big Mouth Billy Bass around under my arm for a year than be seen, by any single person, climbing into or out of a Cybertruck once.
articles.title: Farewell To The Cybertruck, A Total Failure

articles.description:
Bill Simmons got himself into some trouble a few weeks ago, when he admitted on his podcast that he had engaged in proxy betting. Simmons, who lives in California, where online sports gambling is still illegal, told his listeners that he had instructed his daughter's boyfriend, who lives in gambling-friendly Massachusetts, to log into his FanDuel account and place bets on his behalf. Because this practice is strictly prohibited by FanDuel's policies, his bets were voided. But a question remained: How much action was Simmons denied?
Now, thanks to the Massachusetts Gaming Commission, we have an answer to that question. Sports betting reporter Geoff Zochodne pointed out that the commission's Investigation and Enforcement Bureau made a presentation to commissioners Thursday about Simmons's infraction. A memo announcing the presentation provided some details about how much Simmons was trying to bet:
The incident involved an admission made by media personality Bill Simmons on his August 30, 2026, podcast pertaining to his placement of proxy wagers on his FanDuel account in Massachusetts through an acquaintance who was physically present in Massachusetts. FanDuel reported that the matter involved 22 wagers with a total handle of $21,800 placed over three (3) dates: August 5, 2026, August 7, 2026, and August 19, 2026.
articles.title: Now We Know How Much Money Bill Simmons Had His Daughter’s Boyfriend Bet For Him

But it's unlikely that anyone's had a rougher go of it under center this year than the Baltimore Ravens. Already sliding out of the ranks of the contenders, Baltimore was without Lamar Jackson for three punchless games due to an ankle sprain, and then, last weekend, he tore up his thumb on his very first snap in his return. His replacement Snoop Huntley is presentable as far as QB2s go, having been here on and off since 2020; Huntley was then promptly injured in the second quarter, and is out for the season with turf toe.
Just about any NFL team is dead meat after the loss of two quarterbacks, but the Ravens are extra-pungent carrion. Joe Fagnano, an undrafted rookie out of Maine and UConn who walked on and played seven years in college, was the sacrificial lamb for Thursday night's game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. And while I have plenty of sympathy for Fagnano and the Ravens offense for only having a short week to prepare, this was indeed Thursday-ass football.

Four different states put forward ballot measures on Tuesday that, if passed, would either strengthen or create new laws keeping trans children out of school sports. Though the night saw massive Democratic victories, even in typical Republican strongholds like Kansas, Texas, and South Carolina, the four initiatives on the ballot tell a different story.
In two states, Arizona and Nebraska, the language will strengthen bans that were already on the books. In the other two states, Washington and Colorado, voters were asked to create new bans where none existed. As of Thursday, ballot measures in Arizona, Nebraska, and Washington were all projected to pass. Colorado's was too close to call, but the numbers leaned toward passage. Per TransAthlete.com, the passage of all four would bring the number of bans in the country, through either law or policy, up to 31.

This is not the correct time for me to be visiting Sam’s Burgers. It’s the middle of the afternoon here in North Beach, and finding a spot inside Sam’s tight confines isn’t much of a problem. If I were to walk in here 12 hours from now, just before the bars close and after patrons of all the nearby strip clubs have no more rain to make … well then, I probably wouldn’t be able to walk in here at all. There would probably be a line going outside the door. There would probably be an ass parked in every bright red leather stool at the counter and in the scant number of booths lining the wall. There would probably be dozens of hungry partiers, some of them quite famous, crowding into the place to eat a cheeseburger at the proper time to be eating a cheeseburger.

That’s when Anthony Bourdain wo…

articles.description:
If you’re wondering whether there are any good people remaining in the tech sector, or in this country’s ruling class in general, you’d be hard pressed to find a better case study than Craig Newmark. Newmark founded Craigslist.org in San Francisco way back in 1996 and became the sort of accidental billionaire that the early dot-com boom cranked out with seeming regularity. Some of those billionaires went on to become evil (Mark Zuckerberg), and some of them ended up merely becoming rich loud guys (Mark Cuban). Newmark, who ceded his CEO duties at Craigslist shortly after its founding, has endeavored to keep a lower profile, and a lower net worth, than any of them.

To wit: Newmark no longer works with Craigslist at all, and spends the bulk of his time tending to various philanthropic endea…
articles.title: Craiglist's founder on why he left San Francisco and the plans for his billions

articles.description:
Quick: name the best croissant filling. If you’re a basic American like me, you only encounter basic croissant flavors: chocolate, almond, and ham and cheese. These are the norm, and they do the job well if you’re hungry and want to feel 10% more French. But surely, you’ve thought, there must be room for more fillings than that in the American croissant repertoire. Surely there must be a, like, fourth thing we can put into one. 

Reader, I’m pleased to report that I have found one such worthy croissant filling, and it’s nothing you’d guess off the top of your head. But take one bite of it, and you’ll know I’m right. 

The croissant in question is dubbed “brown butter cornmeal twice-baked,” and the bakery that sells it is San Francisco’s Butter & Crumble, owned by chef and self-dubbed “girl…
articles.title: I found one of America's best croissants in San Francisco

You have heard about the two Anthropic employees who, this week, publicly informed America that artificial intelligence could eradicate the whole of humanity within a decade, which is less time than it takes for your average Seamless order to arrive. If these gentlemen, Jacob Coxon and Evan Hubinger, are correct in their assessment, the beginning of our destruction may well have commenced a month ago right here in San Francisco.

The first shot fired in this looming war happened at a seemingly innocuous Cow Hollow storefront known as Andon Market. Back in August, Luna, the AI bot that serves as that store’s manager, fired one of its own employees. The employee in question was dinged by their virtual boss for being late to work, abandoning their post once they got there, and charging snacks…
articles.title: SF's AI-run store is losing money fast. After a visit, I'm not surprised.

articles.description:
There’s a good chance you’ve heard of Tadich Grill, given that the restaurant is older than San Francisco itself. It’s existed in one form or another since 1849, when it opened under the name Coffee Stand. That was one year before the city of San Francisco was formally incorporated, and 118 years before the restaurant moved to its current location on California Street in the Financial District. Tadich has been doling out fresh seafood and mesquite-grilled slabs of meat to patrons through a lifespan that has included multiple earthquakes, two world wars, Prohibition and multiple pandemics. It’s not merely the oldest restaurant in San Francisco, but in all of California. An eternal landmark. I only needed to walk through its doors on an early evening this August to understand why.

Actually,…
articles.title: I tried the $60 cioppino at San Francisco's oldest restaurant

articles.description:
There’s a midterm election coming on Nov. 3, which includes a race here in California to determine who will replace Gov. Gavin Newsom. On the blue side of the ticket is unremarkable Democrat Xavier Becerra, whose chief positive attribute is that he is not a Republican. On the red side is Steve Hilton, an immigrant from the U.K. who gained U.S. citizenship in 2021. Hilton’s most high-profile political experience came back in the early 2010s, when he served as an adviser to then-U.K. prime minister and alleged porcine enthusiast David Cameron. But that experience, plus a lengthy stint as a commentator for Fox News, was enough to convince Hilton that he not only should run for governor, but that he WILL be the state’s next governor.

On the surface, he makes for an attractive candidate. Hilto…
articles.title: Steve Hilton is convinced he's going to win. Hahahaha.

articles.description:
I am not a rock star, although I like to imagine myself as one. I imagine it so, so hard: packed stadiums, crowds numbering five figures going wild as I take my shirt off, shady managers hanging out backstage ready to ply me with Hefty bags full of pharmaceutical cocaine. But it’s too late for me, on the cusp of 50, to actually become a rock star — it certainly couldn’t be a skill or charisma issue, no sir — which is why there’s a tiny slice of the hospitality industry that exists to make patrons like me FEEL like rock stars, if only for a brief moment. 

This is where the legendary Phoenix Hotel, plopped down on Eddy Street right in the middle of San Francisco’s Tenderloin neighborhood, comes in.

I have stayed at many hotels in San Francisco, but all of them were hotel hotels. Elevator b…
articles.title: San Francisco's best hotel cannot be killed

articles.description:
There is exactly one three-starred Michelin-rated Mexican restaurant in the world, and somewhat rudely, it’s not in Mexico. It’s Californios, a $450 prix fixe gastronomic temple tucked away on 11th Street in the SoMa neighborhood of San Francisco. 

You already know this kind of restaurant simply from the price point (which rose $50 since my visit, from $325 to $375 before tax/tip/drinks), and from the fact that it got the notice of the fabled Michelin judges this year, who went so far as to declare it the best Mexican restaurant in the world. Is this the kind of place custom made for its patrons to boast about having dined there? Of course. Does the 12-course tasting menu include fantasy novel ingredients such as “chickweed”? You bet it does. Do certain dishes come with tweezers? Bitch, y…
articles.title: The 'best Mexican restaurant in the world' is in SF. It only cost me $500.

articles.description:
There’s an election next week, which means that you and I are currently being bombarded, ceaselessly, with unwanted voices. Here’s one such voice that, alas, we cannot vote out of office come Tuesday:

That’s ESPN commentator and one-man pandemic Pat McAfee. If you’re unfamiliar with McAfee’s work, I envy you. No seriously, if I could trade bodies with you right now, I’d do it in a heartbeat. I don’t even care if you’re 85 and dying of gonorrhea, I’d still do it. That’s just how much I can’t stand Pat McAfee.
